Read the case and answer the questions accordingly: CO- Ruan, a 24-year-old engineering student from Indore, grew up hearing 1,2,3 phrases like “boys don’t cry” and “real men don’t back down.” In school he was praised for being aggressive in sports and teased his classmates who didn’t fit into the typical “macho” mould. He laughed at sexist jokes without thinking twice. In college, Ruan joined a campus theatre group that staged plays on gender equality and domestic violence. During rehearsals, he was assigned a role portraying an abusive husband — something that made him deeply uncomfortable. Through discussions with his peers, he began realizing how violence and dominance were normalized in the name of masculinity. When Ruan later started dating a classmate, he caught himself feeling insecure about her academic achievements. He admitted to her, “It bothers me that you’re doing better than me,” and was surprised when she replied “That’s exactly what patriarchy teaches you.” Ruan began reading about toxic masculinity and gender communication realizing how often men use humour or silence to mask vulnerability. He also started an online podcast called The Gentle Guy, where he invited men to talk about emotions, consent, and healthy relationships. While some listeners appreciated the honesty, others mocked him, calling him “weak” and “simp.” Even some friends said, “Why talk about gender? That’s women’s stuff.” Over time, Ruan learned that unlearning masculinity was not about rejecting his identity but redefining it — one conversation at a time. How does Ruan’s journey reflect the process of gender 1. socialization and its impact on men? Discuss the concept of toxic masculinity using examples from the 2.   case. How can education and peer discussions promote gender sensitive attitudes among men?
